claims.text: A machine-learning surrogate can be trained on a limited set of high-fidelity ab initio calculations.
The surrogate can accurately reproduce the free energies of both solid and liquid phases.
The surrogate can retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling contributions.
The surrogate will significantly reduce computational cost relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The surrogate will significantly reduce computational cost relative to TOR-TILD.
The approach remains effective for multicomponent high-entropy alloys near fusion conditions.
The proposed scope includes elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys in disordered solid-solution and liquid states.
Special quasi-random structures can represent disordered solid alloy configurations for thermodynamic calculations.
Statistically significant sampling of disordered configurations will capture the relevant features of both solid and liquid states.
Learning an energy landscape from carefully selected ab initio data permits efficient interpolation of alloy energetics.
Interpolation of the learned energy landscape is sufficient to predict full phase free energies, including vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration terms.
The surrogate will produce phase free energies and fusion observables with fidelity comparable to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The throughput advantage will be especially substantial in multicomponent systems.
The method is expected to operate over temperatures below and above the fusion point.
Accuracy and transferability across broad high-entropy-alloy composition and temperature ranges remain unvalidated.
The surrogate can be benchmarked against explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD using solid and liquid phase free energies over a temperature interval spanning fusion.
A deviation greater than 5–10% in phase free energies or derived fusion properties would falsify the proposed replacement fidelity.
Failure to capture key entropy contributions across the phase transition would falsify the hypothesis.
